claim: Accurate tracking of the same neurons across multiple days is crucial for studying changes in neuronal activity during learning and adaptation.
source: Accurate tracking of the same neurons across multiple days is crucial for studying changes in neuronal activity during learning and adaptation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of neuron tracking, supported by established scientific understanding and the context of the research.

claim: Advances in high-density extracellular electrophysiology recording probes, such as Neuropixels, provide a promising avenue to accomplish neuron tracking across multiple days.
source: Advances in high-density extracellular electrophysiology recording probes, such as Neuropixels, provide a promising avenue to accomplish this goal.
evidence: This statement is based on the known capabilities of Neuropixels technology and its application in the field.

claim: Identifying the same neurons in multiple recordings is complicated by non-rigid movement of the tissue relative to the recording sites (drift).
source: Identifying the same neurons in multiple recordings is, however, complicated by non-rigid movement of the tissue relative to the recording sites (drift) and loss of signal from some neurons.
evidence: This is a known challenge in chronic electrophysiology recordings, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Identifying the same neurons in multiple recordings is complicated by loss of signal from some neurons.
source: Identifying the same neurons in multiple recordings is, however, complicated by non-rigid movement of the tissue relative to the recording sites (drift) and loss of signal from some neurons.
evidence: This is a known challenge in chronic electrophysiology recordings, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: The proposed neuron tracking method can identify the same cells independent of firing statistics.
source: Here, we propose a neuron tracking method that can identify the same cells independent of firing statistics, that are used by most existing methods.
evidence: This is a key claim about the method's capability, which is tested and validated in the manuscript through experimental data.

claim: Most existing neuron tracking methods use firing statistics.
source: Here, we propose a neuron tracking method that can identify the same cells independent of firing statistics, that are used by most existing methods.
evidence: This is a statement about the field, supported by citations to existing methods in the Introduction section.

claim: The proposed method is based on between-day non-rigid alignment of spike-sorted clusters.
source: Our method is based on between-day non-rigid alignment of spike-sorted clusters.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, which is detailed in the Methods section.

claim: The same cell identity was verified in mice using measured visual receptive fields.
source: We verified the same cell identity in mice using measured visual receptive fields.
evidence: This describes the validation approach used in the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The method succeeds on datasets separated from 1 to 47 days.
source: This method succeeds on datasets separated from 1 to 47 days, with an 84% average recovery rate.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The method achieves an 84% average recovery rate on datasets separated from 1 to 47 days.
source: This method succeeds on datasets separated from 1 to 47 days, with an 84% average recovery rate.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The ability to longitudinally track neural activity is crucial to understanding central capabilities and changes of neural circuits that operate on long time-scales, such as learning and plasticity.
source: The ability to longitudinally track neural activity is crucial to understanding central capabilities and changes of neural circuits that operate on long time-scales, such as learning and plasticity (Carmena et al., 2005; Clopath et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2012; Liberti et al., 2016), motor stability (Carmena et al., 2005; Dhawale et al., 2017; Jensen et al., 2022), etc.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: The ability to longitudinally track neural activity is crucial to understanding motor stability.
source: The ability to longitudinally track neural activity is crucial to understanding central capabilities and changes of neural circuits that operate on long time-scales, such as learning and plasticity (Carmena et al., 2005; Clopath et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2012; Liberti et al., 2016), motor stability (Carmena et al., 2005; Dhawale et al., 2017; Jensen et al., 2022), etc.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: The authors seek to develop a method capable of tracking single units regardless of changes in functional responses for the duration of an experiment spanning 1–2 months.
source: We seek to develop a method capable of tracking single units regardless of changes in functional responses for the duration of an experiment spanning 1–2 months.
evidence: This is a stated goal of the research.

claim: High-density multi-channel extracellular electrophysiology recording devices enable chronic recordings over large areas for days to months.
source: High-density multi-channel extracellular electrophysiology (ephys) recording devices enable chronic recordings over large areas for days to months (Steinmetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Chronic recordings make possible experiments targeted at improving our understanding of neural computation and underlying mechanisms.
source: Such chronic recordings make possible experiments targeted at improving our understanding of neural computation and underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of chronic recordings, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Examples of neural processes studied with chronic recordings include perceptual decision-making, exploration, and navigation.
source: Examples include perceptual decision-making, exploration, and navigation (Brown et al., 2004; Buzsáki, 2004; Harris, 2005; Harris et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2020; Quian Quiroga and Panzeri, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Electrode arrays with hundreds to thousands of sites, e.g., Neuropixels, are now used extensively to record the neural activity of large populations stably and with high spatio-temporal resolution.
source: Electrode arrays with hundreds to thousands of sites, e.g., Neuropixels, are now used extensively to record the neural activity of large populations stably and with high spatio-temporal resolution, capturing hundreds of neurons with single neuron resolution (Buzsáki, 2004; Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing Neuropixels technology.

claim: Neuropixels can capture hundreds of neurons with single neuron resolution.
source: Electrode arrays with hundreds to thousands of sites, e.g., Neuropixels, are now used extensively to record the neural activity of large populations stably and with high spatio-temporal resolution, capturing hundreds of neurons with single neuron resolution (Buzsáki, 2004; Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing Neuropixels technology.

claim: Electrophysiology retains higher time resolution needed for single spike identification compared with calcium imaging.
source: Moreover, ephys retains the higher time resolution needed for single spike identification, as compared with calcium imaging that provides more spatial cues with which to track neurons over days.
evidence: This is a comparison of two recording modalities based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Calcium imaging provides more spatial cues with which to track neurons over days compared to electrophysiology.
source: Moreover, ephys retains the higher time resolution needed for single spike identification, as compared with calcium imaging that provides more spatial cues with which to track neurons over days.
evidence: This is a comparison of two recording modalities based on established scientific understanding.

claim: The first step in analyzing ephys data is to extract single neuron signals from the recorded voltage traces, i.e., spike sorting.
source: The first step in analyzing ephys data is to extract single neuron signals from the recorded voltage traces, i.e., spike sorting.
evidence: This is a standard procedure in electrophysiology data analysis, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Spike sorting identifies individual neurons by grouping detected action potentials using waveform profiles and amplitudes.
source: Spike sorting identifies individual neurons by grouping detected action potentials using waveform profiles and amplitudes.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting process, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Specific spike sorting algorithms include principal components-based methods.
source: Specific algorithms include principal components-based methods (Quiroga et al., 2004; Chah et al., 2011), and template-matching methods, e.g., Kilosort (Brown et al., 2004; Carlson and Carin, 2019; Harris et al., 2016; Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing these methods.

claim: Specific spike sorting algorithms include template-matching methods, e.g., Kilosort.
source: Specific algorithms include principal components-based methods (Quiroga et al., 2004; Chah et al., 2011), and template-matching methods, e.g., Kilosort (Brown et al., 2004; Carlson and Carin, 2019; Harris et al., 2016; Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing these methods.

claim: Spike sorting is often computationally intensive on large datasets (tens to hundreds of GB).
source: Due to the high-dimensional nature of the data, spike sorting is often computationally intensive on large datasets (tens to hundreds of GB) and optimized to run on single sessions.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of spike sorting algorithms, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Spike sorting is optimized to run on single sessions.
source: Due to the high-dimensional nature of the data, spike sorting is often computationally intensive on large datasets (tens to hundreds of GB) and optimized to run on single sessions.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of spike sorting algorithms, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Processing multiple sessions has received minimal attention in spike sorting.
source: Thus processing multiple sessions has received minimal attention, and the challenges therein remain largely unaddressed.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field, supported by the lack of methods addressing this issue.

claim: The challenges in processing multiple sessions remain largely unaddressed.
source: Thus processing multiple sessions has received minimal attention, and the challenges therein remain largely unaddressed.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field, supported by the lack of methods addressing this issue.

claim: One major challenge in reliably tracking neurons is the potential for changes in the neuron population recorded.
source: One major challenge in reliably tracking neurons is the potential for changes in the neuron population recorded (Figure 1a and Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a stated challenge, illustrated by figures showing neuron positions across days.

claim: The probe is attached to the skull, so brain tissue can move relative to the probe.
source: In particular, since the probe is attached to the skull, brain tissue can move relative to the probe, e.g., during licking, and drift can accumulate over time (Jun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in chronic recordings, supported by a citation.

claim: Brain tissue can move relative to the probe during licking.
source: In particular, since the probe is attached to the skull, brain tissue can move relative to the probe, e.g., during licking, and drift can accumulate over time (Jun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in chronic recordings, supported by a citation.

claim: Drift can accumulate over time in chronic recordings.
source: In particular, since the probe is attached to the skull, brain tissue can move relative to the probe, e.g., during licking, and drift can accumulate over time (Jun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in chronic recordings, supported by a citation.

claim: Kilosort 2.5 corrects drift within a single recording by inferring tissue motion from continuous changes in spiking activity and interpolating the data to account for that motion.
source: Kilosort 2.5 corrects drift within a single recording by inferring tissue motion from continuous changes in spiking activity and interpolating the data to account for that motion (Steinmetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a feature of Kilosort 2.5, supported by a citation.

claim: Larger between-recording drift occurs for sessions on different days.
source: Larger between-recording drift occurs for sessions on different days, and can (1) change the size and location of spike waveforms along the probe (Hall et al., 2021), (2) lose neurons that move out of range, and (3) gain new neurons that move into recording range.
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in chronic recordings, supported by a citation.

claim: Between-recording drift can change the size and location of spike waveforms along the probe.
source: Larger between-recording drift occurs for sessions on different days, and can (1) change the size and location of spike waveforms along the probe (Hall et al., 2021), (2) lose neurons that move out of range, and (3) gain new neurons that move into recording range.
evidence: This is a known phenomenon in chronic recordings, supported by a citation.

claim: Between-recording drift can lose neurons that move out of range.
source: Larger between-recording drift occurs for sessions on different days, and can (1) change the size and location of spike waveforms along the probe (Hall et al., 2021), (2) lose neurons that move out of range, and (3) gain new neurons that move into recording range.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of tissue movement relative to the probe.

claim: Between-recording drift can gain new neurons that move into recording range.
source: Larger between-recording drift occurs for sessions on different days, and can (1) change the size and location of spike waveforms along the probe (Hall et al., 2021), (2) lose neurons that move out of range, and (3) gain new neurons that move into recording range.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of tissue movement relative to the probe.

claim: Clusters can change firing pattern characteristics or completely appear/disappear across recordings.
source: Thus clusters can change firing pattern characteristics or completely appear/disappear.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the drift and neuron loss/gain described previously.

claim: The specific firing patterns classified as unit clusters may appear and disappear in different recordings.
source: As a result the specific firing patterns classified as unit clusters may appear and disappear in different recordings (Bar-Hillel et al., 2006; Harris et al., 2016; Swindale and Spacek, 2014; Tolias et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Another challenge is that popular template-matching-based spike-sorting methods usually involve some randomness in template initialization.
source: Another challenge is that popular template-matching-based spike-sorting methods usually involve some randomness in template initialization (Chung et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2020; Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing these methods.

claim: As a result of randomness in template initialization, action potentials can be assigned into clusters differently across runs.
source: As a result, action potentials can be assigned into clusters differently, and clusters can be merged or separated differently across runs.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the randomness in template initialization.

claim: As a result of randomness in template initialization, clusters can be merged or separated differently across runs.
source: As a result, action potentials can be assigned into clusters differently, and clusters can be merged or separated differently across runs.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the randomness in template initialization.

claim: Previous neuron tracking methods are frequently based on waveform and firing statistics.
source: Previous neuron tracking methods are frequently based on waveform and firing statistics, e.g., firing rate similarity (Chung et al., 2019), action potential shape correlation, and inter-spike interval (ISI) histogram shape (Vasil'eva et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing these methods.

claim: When neuronal representations change, e.g., during learning or representational drift, neural activity statistics become less reliable for tracking.
source: When neuronal representations change, e.g., during learning (Carmena et al., 2005; Huber et al., 2012; Liberti et al., 2016) or representational drift (Rokni et al., 2007), neural activity statistics became less reliable.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and logical reasoning.

claim: The proposed method takes advantage of the rich spatial-temporal information in the multi-channel recordings.
source: In this work, we take advantage of the rich spatial-temporal information in the multi-channel recordings, matching units based on the estimated neuron locations, and unit waveforms (Lewicki, 1998), instead of firing patterns.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The proposed method matches units based on the estimated neuron locations and unit waveforms instead of firing patterns.
source: In this work, we take advantage of the rich spatial-temporal information in the multi-channel recordings, matching units based on the estimated neuron locations, and unit waveforms (Lewicki, 1998), instead of firing patterns.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: Steinmetz et al., 2021, concatenated pairs of datasets after low-resolution alignment.
source: As an alternative method, Steinmetz et al., 2021, concatenated pairs of datasets after low-resolution alignment, awkward for more than two datasets.
evidence: This describes a prior method, supported by a citation.

claim: The concatenation method of Steinmetz et al., 2021 is awkward for more than two datasets.
source: As an alternative method, Steinmetz et al., 2021, concatenated pairs of datasets after low-resolution alignment, awkward for more than two datasets.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of the prior method.

claim: The reported tracking method is more flexible, expandable, and robust than the concatenation method.
source: We report here a more flexible, expandable, and robust tracking method that can track neurons effectively and efficiently across any number of sessions.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the proposed method, supported by the experimental results.

claim: The reported tracking method can track neurons effectively and efficiently across any number of sessions.
source: We report here a more flexible, expandable, and robust tracking method that can track neurons effectively and efficiently across any number of sessions.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the proposed method, supported by the experimental results.

claim: The datasets consist of multiple recordings taken from three mice over 2 months.
source: Our datasets consist of multiple recordings taken from three mice (Figure 7a) over 2 months.
evidence: This describes the experimental dataset used in the study.

claim: The time gap between two recordings ranges from 2 to 25 days.
source: The time gap between two recordings ranges from 2 to 25 days.
evidence: This describes the experimental dataset used in the study.

claim: Each dataset is spike-sorted individually with a standard Kilosort 2.5 pipeline.
source: Each dataset is spike-sorted individually with a standard Kilosort 2.5 pipeline.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure used in the study.

claim: The sorting results are post-processed using ecephys spike sorting pipeline.
source: The sorting results, including unit assignment, spike times, etc., are used as input for our method (post-processed using ecephys spike sorting pipeline; Colonell, 2018) (section Dataset).
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: No manual curation was performed to ensure the sorting results are unbiased.
source: To ensure the sorting results are unbiased, we performed no manual curation.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to avoid bias.

claim: Only the subset of units labeled as 'good' by Kilosort (KSgood units) were considered.
source: As the clusters returned by Kilosort can vary in quality, we only considered the subset of units labeled as 'good' by Kilosort, here referred to as KSgood units (section Reference set).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice for quality control.

claim: KSgood units are mainly determined by the amount of ISI violations.
source: KSgood units are mainly determined by the amount of ISI violations and are believed to represent a single unit (Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the criteria for KSgood units, supported by a citation.

claim: KSgood units are believed to represent a single unit.
source: KSgood units are mainly determined by the amount of ISI violations and are believed to represent a single unit (Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of KSgood units, supported by a citation.

claim: The overall strategy is to run spike sorting once per session, and then to generate a unit-by-unit assignment between pairs of datasets.
source: Our overall strategy is to run spike sorting once per session, and then to generate a unit-by-unit assignment between pairs of datasets.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: When tracking units across more than two sessions, two strategies are possible: match all ensuing sessions to a single session or match consecutive pairs of sessions and then trace matched units through all sessions.
source: When tracking units across more than two sessions, two strategies are possible: match all ensuing sessions to a single session (e.g. the first session) (section Measuring rigid drift using the EMD and section Determining z-distance threshold), or match consecutive pairs of sessions and then trace matched units through all sessions (section Units can be tracked in discontinuous recordings for 48 days).
evidence: This describes the methodological options for multi-session tracking.

claim: Reference units are the subset of KSgood units with strong and distinguishable visual responses in both datasets of a comparison.
source: We refer to the subset of KSgood units with strong and distinguishable visual responses in both datasets of a comparison as reference units (see section Reference set for details).
evidence: This defines a key term used in the study.

claim: Unit matching of reference units was validated using visual receptive field similarity, similar to Steinmetz et al., 2021.
source: Similar to Steinmetz et al., 2021, we validated our unit matching of reference units using visual receptive field similarity.
evidence: This describes the validation approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: Trackable units with strong visual responses are qualitatively similar to those without.
source: Finally, we showed that trackable units with strong visual responses are qualitatively similar to those without (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 to Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The earth mover's distance (EMD) was used to provide registration between pairs of recordings.
source: To provide registration between pairs of recordings, we used the earth mover's distance (EMD) (Bertrand et al., 2020; Cohen, 1999).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, supported by citations.

claim: A feature space consisting of a geometric distance space and a waveform similarity space is used to address both rigid and non-rigid neuron motion.
source: We use a feature space consisting of a geometric distance space and a waveform similarity space, to address both rigid and non-rigid neuron motion.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The EMD finds matches between objects in the two distributions by minimizing the overall distances between the established matches.
source: The EMD finds matches between objects in the two distributions by minimizing the overall distances between the established matches (section Earth mover's distance).
evidence: This describes the EMD algorithm, supported by citations in the referenced section.

claim: EMD is used in two stages: rigid drift correction and unit assignment.
source: We use EMD in two stages: rigid drift correction and unit assignment.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The EMD incorporates two parameters crucial for matching units: location-based physical distance and a waveform distance metric.
source: Importantly, the EMD incorporates two parameters crucial for matching units: location-based physical distance and a waveform distance metric that characterizes similarity of waveforms (section Calculating the EMD metric).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The first EMD stage estimates the homogeneous vertical movement of the entire population of KSgood units.
source: The first EMD stage estimates the homogeneous vertical movement of the entire population of KSgood units (Figure 2b).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, illustrated in a figure.

claim: The rigid drift estimation procedure is illustrated in Figure 2b.
source: The rigid drift estimation procedure is illustrated in Figure 2b.
evidence: This refers to a figure that illustrates the procedure.

claim: Post drift correction, a unit's true match will be close in both physical distance and waveform distance.
source: Post drift correction, a unit's true match will be close in both physical distance and waveform distance.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the drift correction procedure.

claim: Drift-corrected units were matched at the second EMD stage.
source: Drift-corrected units were then matched at the second EMD stage.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The EMD between assigned units can be thought of as the local non-rigid drift combined with the waveform distortion resulting from drift.
source: The EMD between assigned units can be thought of as the local non-rigid drift combined with the waveform distortion resulting from drift.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EMD metric in the context of the study.

claim: The accuracy of the matching was tested by comparing with reference unit assignments based on visual receptive fields.
source: We test the accuracy of the matching by comparing with reference unit assignments based on visual receptive fields (section Reference set).
evidence: This describes the validation approach used in the study.

claim: For each unit, the location is determined by fitting the peak-to-peak amplitudes on the 10 sites nearest the site with peak signal, based on the triangulation method in Boussard et al., 2021.
source: For each unit, the location is determined by fitting the peak-to-peak amplitudes on the 10 sites nearest the site with peak signal, based on the triangulation method in Boussard et al., 2021 (section Calculating the EMD metric).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach, supported by a citation.

claim: The waveform distance is an L2 norm between two spatial-temporal waveforms that spans 22 channels and 2.7 ms.
source: The waveform distance is an L2 norm between two spatial-temporal waveforms that spans 22 channels and 2.7 ms (section Calculating the EMD metric).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: Physical unit distances provide a way to maintain the internal structure and relations between units in the EMD.
source: Physical unit distances provide a way to maintain the internal structure and relations between units in the EMD.
evidence: This is a rationale for using physical distances in the EMD.

claim: Waveform similarity metrics will distinguish units in the local neighborhood and likely reduce the effect of new and missing units.
source: Waveform similarity metrics will distinguish units in the local neighborhood and likely reduce the effect of new and missing units.
evidence: This is a rationale for using waveform similarity in the EMD.

claim: The match assignment results were analyzed in two ways.
source: We analyzed the match assignment results in two ways.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach of the study.

claim: All subsequent datasets were compared to dataset 1 using recovery rate and accuracy.
source: First, we compared all subsequent datasets to dataset 1 using recovery rate and accuracy.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach of the study.

claim: The EMD forces all units from the dataset with fewer neurons to have an assigned match.
source: Since the EMD forces all units from the dataset with fewer neurons to have an assigned match, we use vertical z-distance to threshold out the biologically impossible unit assignments.
evidence: This describes a property of the EMD algorithm.

claim: Vertical z-distance is used to threshold out biologically impossible unit assignments.
source: Since the EMD forces all units from the dataset with fewer neurons to have an assigned match, we use vertical z-distance to threshold out the biologically impossible unit assignments.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to improve accuracy.

claim: Non-reference units are matched units without receptive field information but whose z-distance is smaller than the threshold.
source: We also retrieved non-reference units, i.e., matched units without receptive field information but whose z-distance is smaller than the threshold.
evidence: This defines a category of units analyzed in the study.

claim: Units were tracked between consecutive datasets and the waveforms, unit locations, firing rates, and visual responses of all tracked chains were summarized and analyzed.
source: Second, we tracked units between consecutive datasets and summarized and analyzed the waveforms, unit locations, firing rates, and visual responses (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 to Figure 5 for details) of all tracked chains, i.e., units which can be tracked across at least three consecutive datasets.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach of the study.

claim: Chains are units which can be tracked across at least three consecutive datasets.
source: Second, we tracked units between consecutive datasets and summarized and analyzed the waveforms, unit locations, firing rates, and visual responses (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 to Figure 5 for details) of all tracked chains, i.e., units which can be tracked across at least three consecutive datasets.
evidence: This defines a key term used in the study.

claim: Drift happens mostly along the direction of probe insertion (vertical or z-direction).
source: Drift happens mostly along the direction of probe insertion (vertical or z-direction).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of drift in chronic recordings, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: The amount of vertical drift is estimated under the assumption that part of the drift is rigid.
source: We want to estimate the amount of vertical drift under the assumption that part of the drift is rigid; this is likely a good assumption given the small (≈720 μm) z-range of these recordings.
evidence: This describes a methodological assumption, justified by the small recording range.

claim: The assumption that part of the drift is rigid is likely a good assumption given the small (≈720 μm) z-range of these recordings.
source: We want to estimate the amount of vertical drift under the assumption that part of the drift is rigid; this is likely a good assumption given the small (≈720 μm) z-range of these recordings.
evidence: This justifies a methodological assumption based on the experimental setup.

claim: The EMD allows extraction of the homogeneous (rigid) movement of matched units.
source: The EMD allows us to extract the homogeneous (rigid) movement of matched units.
evidence: This describes a capability of the EMD algorithm in the context of the study.

claim: Only ≈60% of units are detected across pairs of days in the analyzed data.
source: In the real data analyzed here, we find that only ≈60% of units are detected across pairs of days, so the rigid motion of the real pairs must be detected against a background of units with no true match.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Units with no real match will have z-shifts far from the consensus z-shift of the paired units.
source: In the real data analyzed here, we find that only ≈60% of units are detected across pairs of days, so the rigid motion of the real pairs must be detected against a background of units with no true match. These units with no real match will have z-shifts far from the consensus z-shift of the paired units (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the rigid drift assumption, illustrated in a figure.

claim: In Figure 2, a 12 µm upward drift was added to the z-coordinate of the units from the second day to demonstrate detection of significant drift.
source: To demonstrate detection of significant drift, we added a 12 µm upward drift to the z-coordinate of the units from the second day.
evidence: This describes a manipulation performed for demonstration purposes.

claim: The first stage of the EMD is used to find matches using the combined distance metric.
source: The first stage of the EMD is used to find matches using the combined distance metric as described in section Calculating the EMD metric.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The EMD assigns matches to all units in the smaller dataset regardless of biophysical plausibility.
source: As the EMD is an optimization algorithm with no biological constraints, it assigns matches to all units in the smaller dataset regardless of biophysical plausibility.
evidence: This describes a property of the EMD algorithm.

claim: Some of the assigned matches may have unrealistically long distances.
source: As a result, some of the assigned matches may have unrealistically long distances.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the EMD assigning all matches.

claim: A distance threshold is required to select correct pairs.
source: A distance threshold is therefore required to select correct pairs.
evidence: This is a methodological necessity to improve accuracy.

claim: For the illustration in Figure 2, the threshold is set to 15 μm.
source: For the illustration in Figure 2, the threshold is set to 15 μm, which is chosen to be larger than most of the z-shifts observed in our experimental data.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice for the demonstration.

claim: The 15 μm threshold was chosen to be larger than most of the z-shifts observed in the experimental data.
source: For the illustration in Figure 2, the threshold is set to 15 μm, which is chosen to be larger than most of the z-shifts observed in our experimental data.
evidence: This justifies the choice of threshold based on the data.

claim: The threshold value will be refined later by distribution fitting (Figure 4).
source: The threshold value will be refined later by distribution fitting (Figure 4).
evidence: This indicates a future step in the analysis.

claim: In Figure 2, all of the sub-threshold (short) distances belong to upward pairs.
source: In Figure 2 all of the sub-threshold (short) distances belong to upward pairs (Figure 2b and c, red solid arrows), showing that the EMD can detect the homogeneous movement direction and the amount of imposed drift.
evidence: This is an observation from the demonstration, shown in the figure.

claim: The EMD can detect the homogeneous movement direction and the amount of imposed drift.
source: In Figure 2 all of the sub-threshold (short) distances belong to upward pairs (Figure 2b and c, red solid arrows), showing that the EMD can detect the homogeneous movement direction and the amount of imposed drift.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the demonstration, supported by the data shown in the figure.

claim: When determining matched reference units from visual response data, units are required to be spatially nearby (within 30 μm) as well as having similar visual responses.
source: When determining matched reference units from visual response data, we require that units be spatially nearby (within 30 μm) as well as having similar visual responses.
evidence: This describes the criteria for reference unit matching.

claim: After correcting for drift, more reference units are recovered.
